verses.text: When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister. She said to Jacob, “Give me children, or else I will die.”
Jacob’s anger burned against Rachel, and he said, “Am I in God’s place, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?”
She said, “Behold, my maid Bilhah. Go in to her, that she may bear on my knees, and I also may obtain children by her.”
She gave him Bilhah her servant as wife, and Jacob went in to her.
Bilhah conceived, and bore Jacob a son.
Rachel said, “God has judged me, and has also heard my voice, and has given me a son.” Therefore called she his name Dan.
Bilhah, Rachel’s servant, conceived again, and bore Jacob a second son.
Rachel said, “I have wrestled with my sister with mighty wrestlings, and have prevailed.” She named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had finished bearing, she took Zilpah, her servant, and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, “How fortunate!” She named him Gad.
Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, “Happy am I, for the daughters will call me happy.” She named him Asher.
Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them to his mother, Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

She said to her, “Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Would you take away my son’s mandrakes, also?” Rachel said, “Therefore he will lie with you tonight for your son’s mandrakes.”
Jacob came from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him, and said, “You must come in to me; for I have surely hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” He lay with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she conceived, and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, “God has given me my hire, because I gave my servant to my husband.” She named him Issachar.
Leah conceived again, and bore a sixth son to Jacob.
Leah said, “God has endowed me with a good dowry. Now my husband will live with me, because I have borne him six sons.” She named him Zebulun.
Afterwards, she bore a daughter, and named her Dinah.
God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her, and opened her womb.
She conceived, bore a son, and said, “God has taken away my reproach.”
She named him Joseph,  saying, “May Yahweh add another son to me.”
When Rachel had borne Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, “Send me away, that I may go to my own place, and to my country.
Give me my wives and my children for whom I have served you, and let me go; for you know my service with which I have served you.”
Laban said to him, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, stay here, for I have divined that Yahweh has blessed me for your sake.”
He said, “Appoint me your wages, and I will give it.”
He said to him, “You know how I have served you, and how your livestock have fared with me.
For it was little which you had before I came, and it has increased to a multitude. Yahweh has blessed you wherever I turned. Now when will I provide for my own house also?”
He said, “What shall I give you?” Jacob said, “You shall not give me anything. If you will do this thing for me, I will again feed your flock and keep it.
I will pass through all your flock today, removing from there every speckled and spotted one, and every black one among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats. This will be my hire.

So my righteousness will answer for me hereafter, when you come concerning my hire that is before you. Every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats, and black among the sheep, that might be with me, will be considered stolen.”
Laban said, “Behold, let it be according to your word.”

That day, he removed the male goats that were streaked and spotted, and all the female goats that were speckled and spotted, every one that had white in it, and all the black ones among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons.
He set three days’ journey between himself and Jacob, and Jacob fed the rest of Laban’s flocks.
Jacob took to himself rods of fresh poplar, almond, plane tree, peeled white streaks in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.
He set the rods which he had peeled opposite the flocks in the gutters in the watering-troughs where the flocks came to drink. They conceived when they came to drink.
The flocks conceived before the rods, and the flocks produced streaked, speckled, and spotted.
Jacob separated the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the streaked and all the black in the flock of Laban: and he put his own droves apart, and didn’t put them into Laban’s flock.
Whenever the stronger of the flock conceived, Jacob laid the rods in front of the eyes of the flock in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods;
but when the flock were feeble, he didn’t put them in. So the feebler were Laban’s, and the stronger Jacob’s.
The man increased exceedingly, and had large flocks, female servants and male servants, and camels and donkeys.

footnotes.content: Rachel's cry is raw: “Give me children, or else I will die.” I have lived long enough to know that envy rarely speaks quietly - it looks at another's blessing and calls it our own deprivation. Yet even this desperate prayer is not hidden from God, who hears the ache beneath our worst words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob answers with truth and with heat: “Am I in God's place, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?” He is right that God opens the womb, but his anger lands on the wrong heart. I have learned to be slow with answers when someone is grieving - sometimes the kindest thing is to carry the question to God together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rachel speaks the household custom of her day: a servant's child born “on my knees” was counted as the mistress's own. It is the same road Sarah walked with Hagar before her. The custom was real, but so was the sorrow that made her reach for it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rachel gives Bilhah to Jacob, and the text tells it plainly, without applause. I notice how quickly a plan meant to ease pain can bind three people tighter. Even so, God does not walk away from the tangle we make.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bilhah conceives and bears a son, and for a moment the house is quiet. I think of all the waiting that came before this small headline. God's kindness often arrives in a single ordinary sentence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rachel names him Dan - “judged” - and says God has heard her voice. She feels vindicated more than rested, and I understand that. The Lord is patient with prayers that are still mostly wounds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bilhah bears a second son, and the story does not slow down for us. I am struck that God keeps giving life in a household that is competing for it. His mercy is not held back by our mess.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The name Naphtali comes from her word for wrestling - she says she has wrestled mightily with her sister and prevailed. It is a strange thing to name a child after a fight. Yet God has always met His people in the wrestling, and He has never turned away from a limp.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah, having stopped bearing, takes the same road and gives Zilpah to Jacob. I wish I could say the rivalry had cooled, but it has only changed hands. How much of our striving is really a hunger to be seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zilpah bears a son, and Leah's household grows again. The text keeps count for us, son by son. Heaven was counting too, and not only the numbers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah names him Gad - “How fortunate!” - and the word sounds like relief. I have known that breath of gratitude when something finally goes right. It is a good thing to say out loud, even if the fortune is smaller than we hoped.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zilpah bears a second son, and the quiet competition continues in the next room. I find it comforting that God's promises to Jacob do not depend on this family sorting itself out first. He works in houses like ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asher means happy, and Leah says the daughters will call her happy. She is reaching for a joy that others can see. The deeper joy, I have found, is the one God gives when no one is watching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuben, still a boy, finds mandrakes in the field at wheat harvest and brings them to his mother. These were the dudaim of the old world, prized in folk belief as a help for barrenness. It is a tender, sad little scene - a child's gift caught up in a grown woman's longing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah's answer carries years of hurt: “Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Would you take away my son's mandrakes, also?” Then Rachel trades a night with Jacob for the plants. I ache at how love and leverage get tangled when we are starving for affection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah goes out to meet Jacob in the evening and tells him plainly that she has hired him with her son's mandrakes. There is something both bold and undignified in it. God does not turn away from this house, and He does not turn away from ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God listened to Leah - the unloved one, the one who thought she had been passed over. She conceives and bears a fifth son. I never tire of this sentence; the Lord has a particular ear for those who feel unheard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She names him Issachar, from the word for hire, because God has given her her hire. Her theology is a little tangled, but her gratitude is real. God accepts the thanks we can manage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah conceives again and bears a sixth son. The story moves quickly now, but each life is a whole world to God. He is not bored by the ordinary arrival of another child.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebulun's name plays on dowry and honor - Leah hopes that now her husband will live with her. She has borne six sons and is still asking to be loved. It is one of the most human lines in Genesis, and one of the most hopeful, because God keeps giving anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Afterward Leah bears a daughter and names her Dinah. She is the only daughter named in this chapter, and the text pauses for her. I am glad she is remembered; she will matter greatly in the story to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her, and opened her womb. Readers today hear an echo of every long prayer that seemed to go unanswered, and of the God who arrives on His own timetable. As of 2026-10, I am grateful that remembering is something God does, not something we must earn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rachel says God has taken away my reproach, and she is right. In her world childlessness was a public shame, and God lifted it. He is gentle with the things that make us hang our heads.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She names him Joseph, from the prayer “May Yahweh add another son to me.” Her longing is not finished - she is already asking for more. Faith sometimes looks like gratitude with an outstretched hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: With Joseph born, Jacob says, “Send me away, that I may go to my own place, and to my country.” After fourteen years he is naming home again. I hear in it the quiet courage of a man who has served long and now dares to ask for his own life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob asks for his wives and children, naming the service he has given for them. He is not demanding a gift; he is asking for what was promised. There is a proper dignity in remembering what God has enabled us to earn and in asking for it plainly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban says he has divined that Yahweh blessed him for Jacob's sake. It is striking - a man who keeps household gods still credits the God of his nephew. Even an unwilling witness can see where the blessing comes from.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban simply says, “Appoint me your wages, and I will give it.” After all the years of being outmaneuvered, Jacob is finally invited to name a price. I notice that God can open a door through the very man who has been shutting them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob answers, “You know how I have served you, and how your livestock have fared with me.” He does not boast; he simply tells the truth. It is good to let our work speak, and better still to leave the outcome with God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob says that what Laban had was little before he came, and now it is a multitude, blessed wherever he turned. Then he asks his honest question: “When will I provide for my own house also?” That is not greed; it is the cry of a man who has cared for others long enough to be allowed to care for his own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: “What shall I give you?” Jacob answers, “You shall not give me anything,” and offers to keep tending the flock. It is a surprising move, and I have learned to respect it. Sometimes freedom begins not with taking a gift but with naming a fair arrangement.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob asks for the speckled, spotted, and black animals as his hire. Those were the minority in the flock, so the offer looked generous to Laban and risky to Jacob. He is trusting God with a small share rather than grasping at a large one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob says his righteousness will answer for him later - any unmarked animal in his hands will count as stolen. He is putting his integrity where his future is, and inviting scrutiny. I wish more of us would let our honesty be audited.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban says, “Behold, let it be according to your word,” and the bargain is struck. It sounds fair on the surface. I have learned to watch what happens after a fair-sounding word, because that is where character shows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That same day Laban removes every streaked, spotted, and black animal and hands them to his own sons. He has agreed to the terms and immediately tilted the field. It is a hard lesson in dealing with someone who keeps moving the fence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban sets three days' journey between himself and Jacob. The distance tells the truth about the trust between them. Yet God is not limited by the miles men put between each other.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob takes fresh rods of poplar, almond, and plane, peels white streaks in them, and sets them where the flocks drink. It was the husbandry of his age, and the text reports it without endorsing it as magic. Whatever Jacob thought the stripes would do, it was God who gave the increase.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He places the peeled rods in the watering troughs where the flocks come to drink and conceive. There is something almost childlike in the careful arrangement. I am reminded how often we do our small part with great seriousness and then depend on God for what only He can do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The flocks conceive before the rods and bear streaked, speckled, and spotted young. The account says it plainly, and I do not need to explain away what God did. He is free to work through means we would not have chosen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob separates the lambs and turns the faces of the flock toward the streaked and black animals of Laban's flock. He is building his own herd carefully, one generation at a time. Patience with small steps is its own kind of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the stronger animals conceive, Jacob sets the rods before them; when the weak ones come, he leaves them alone. The text is candid about his method. It is a reminder that even a blessed man can be shrewd, and that God's purposes are not undone by our cleverness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So the feeble animals go to Laban and the strong ones to Jacob. I wince a little at how neatly it works in Jacob's favor. God had promised to be with him, but the promise does not make every part of his dealings spotless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man increases exceedingly - large flocks, servants, camels, and donkeys. The one who fled home with a staff now has a household of his own. I see God's faithfulness here, and I also see how much of it came through years of hard, unglamorous work. That is usually how promises grow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
